newsitem.title: USA: White House optimistic about U.S. House China vote.
newsitem.headline: White House optimistic about U.S. House China vote.

text.p: The Clinton administration expressed optimism on Tuesday that Congress would support normal trade relations with China as a key House of Representatives panel prepared to vote this week on the measure.
"I think there is reason for cautious optimism all around," Undersecretary of State Stuart Eizenstat said ahead of a congressional hearing on the issue.

The House Ways and Means Committee is scheduled to vote on Wednesday on a resolution that would overturn U.S. President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trade status.

Although a majority of members of the influential Ways and Means committee support normal trade relations with China, they are expected to vote to send the measure to the full House for a vote next week. But they are also expected to recommend that their fellow lawmakers reject it.

The resolution is sponsored by House Rules Committee Chairman Jerry Solomon, a New York Republican who argues that the United States should deny China MFN because of concerns about supression of religious worship and other human rights abuses.
"If ever a policy were out of touch with reality, it is our current policy of appeasement toward Communist China," he said in testimony to the House Ways and Means trade subcommittee.
Eizenstat told reporters he had been canvassing members of the House for support and that he was "encouraged" by calls to both Republicans and Democrats.

Eizenstat said China MFN was in an even stronger position in the Senate, despite Majority Leader Trent Lott's comments on Sunday that it could be in trouble in the Senate because of concerns about a probe into allegations that China tried to influence U.S. elections through illegal contributions.

Administration officials and China MFN supporters hope that the resolution to overturn Clinton's decision will be defeated in the House. If it is defeated there, the issue is unlikely to go forward in the Senate.
Despite its name, Most Favoured Nation trade status is enjoyed by most countries. Only a handful of countries are denied MFN status.

Without it, import tariffs on goods made in China would soar to the high levels of the 1930's. Administration officials have said that tariffs would rise on Chinese imports to an average 40 percent, compared to about six percent currently.
Efforts in Congress to overturn the president on MFN have been unsuccessful since the 1989 Chinese army's bloody crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square.
